title: Napoleon's way of war
note: Napoleon turned the mass armies of the French Revolution into fast, flexible instruments. Self-contained corps marched apart and concentrated to fight; he struck at an enemy's flank, rear or communications, or slipped between two armies to beat each in turn. His downfall in Russia and Spain showed how speed and battle fail against distance, supply and popular resistance.

read.title: How Napoleon won and lost
text: Napoleon inherited an army transformed by the French Revolution. Mass conscription, the levée en masse of 1793, gave France far more soldiers than the old monarchies, and promotion by merit gave it young, aggressive officers. Napoleon organized this mass into corps, each a small army of infantry, cavalry and artillery able to fight on its own for a day until help arrived.

The corps let him spread out to move fast and live off the country, then converge on the decisive point. At Ulm in 1805 his corps swung around behind an Austrian army and forced it to surrender almost without a battle. Weeks later at Austerlitz he left his right wing deliberately weak, tempted the Austrians and Russians to attack it, and then smashed their weakened center. When facing two enemies, he liked to drive between them and beat each in turn.

The same methods had limits. In Spain, a popular guerrilla war tied down French armies for years. In Russia in 1812, distance, hunger, disease and winter destroyed the Grande Armée more surely than any battle. His enemies also learned to copy him, and in 1813 and 1815 they massed coalitions that his genius could not outweigh.
